Even the pink-faced, red-turbaned monster looks uncomfortably insecure on the seeming foundation of the fragile little dwellings huddled at its base. Yet the owner of the monster came to live among the fragile dwellings because he thought them beautiful! How could he then destroy them? What can be done about it is not very clear, since each house-builder has the right to build what house he pleases!

If each of us in every town would care something about the unity of the streets we live on, the towns of America would be the most beautiful in the world. But a haphazard collection of unrelated styles of architecture can never look anything but mongrel. Just go and look at them! Spanish, English, Colonial, Rococo, Byzantine, Italian, German, French, and the uncompromising cube plainness of the new monolith — parading down a whole street length — discord if there ever was discord! Perhaps the only way to create a town of beautiful accord would be to start with a brand-

new development and lay out its streets with restrictions of each, to the type of its name.

COULD IT BE DONE?

Washington Road would be all old Colonial. Via Appia would be Italian. On Old Norman Road, English cottage and Norman peasant might mix quite nicely. In such a town the Browns or the Perugis or the Latours choose the style of house suitable to their ancestors or their taste, and buy a lot in the midst of neighbors whose houses will be in unity with their own. Makeshift Way could be a segregated section for any sort of near-type house of untraceable pedigree, with permanent corners for those who cannot be trusted to keep their architecture the required percentage pure.

The above suggestion is not written in jest. One need merely bring to mind the beauty of French New Orleans, or the enchantment of so many New England or Southern houses that are so truly lovely because the type of old Colonial pervades the entire place; in fact, having a personal preference for Colonial, I myself live half the year in an enchanting New England seacoast town where a whitepainted, green-shuttered and flower-bordered house of my own is duplicated by all its uncles and its cousins and its aunts!

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
section: If You Are Going to Build
text:
/F you are a prospective house-owner, three courses are open to you: you can build, you can remodel, or you can buy ready-made. The advantage if you build is that you can decide upon each separate detail of design, so as to suit your taste and requirements. The disadvantage is that you have to pay for the house as its construction progresses, and yet are homeless throughout the time it is building; moreover, it cannot be seen except "on paper,” which is, for some people, difficult. There is also a popular belief that all custom-made articles are of high cost (not necessarily true) , and that the final cost of house-building is always more than you think it is going to be (99 times out of 100, true) .

On the other hand, if you buy a new house (or an apartment) ready-made, the advantages are, that you can see it actually without having to imagine what it will look like; that you can move into it at once; and that you know exactly what it is going to cost. The disadvantages are, that it is "as built”; that you must judge it by appearance only; and that its price is not — value for value — likely to be economical.

The cost of a house that you build ought to be less than the price of a house put up by a building corporation, because, although building in quantity is cheaper, the profit to the promoter — which includes not merely principal and interest on the money he has put into it, but also reasonable compensation for risk — must almost necessarily raise the total to a higher figure than the cost of building for yourself ought to reach.

The third course — that of remodeling — is becoming every year more popular. In addition to the beautification of full-grown — even if neglected — shrubs and trees, the ad-

vantage of buying an old house, especially one out of repair, is that you can usually buy it for a song. The disadvantage is the uncertainty as to how much the song; may mount up to by the time the renovations are completed. If no structural changes are necessary beyond the putting in of a partition or two and a small amount of plumbing, estimate of improvement and repair is simple enough. But the moment you begin tearing down — that is another story (which will be discussed at length in the next chapter) . Meanwhile, let us begin with the problems of building:

If you have found a site that you like, you have perhaps already visualized the style of house you want to put on it. Perhaps you know so definitely the house you want that you are thinking of building without an architect. Of course, if the house is to be very simple and unpretentious; if you have had a certain amount of experience in building; if the new house is to resemble others in the neighborhood; and, finally, if you have a reliable contractor, he may be able to produce the ideas you have in mind. Or you may be able to do your own designing; or perhaps you are buying ready-made plans which can be used as they are, or modified slightly to suit your requirements.

But under normal circumstances, no matter how well you think you know what you want, the wisdom of engaging an architect cannot be overemphasized. Not merely because the architect is likely to make a more beautiful house, but because, in spite of his ten-per-cent.-over-all fee, the chances are greatly in favor of your saving money in the end.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
House-building is not a simple process for the inexpert. The details that come up for decision are unceasing, and more often than not they involve conundrums which only the technical expert can answer. And if you "guess wrong” the result is ugliness, inconvenience, unsuitability, or that most wasteful of all extravagances, tearing down and doing over.

A good architect foresees the difficulties, saves the redoing here, the wasteful and unnecessary outlay there; he sees, from the first setting up of the frame, that the outline of the building is right. If something seems wrong, he does not "hope it will look better later on.” He knows either that it will or that it won’t, and in the latter case he adjusts it at the beginning. He also sees that the materials used are those which the specifications call for, and that each detail of the house is assembled as it should be, straight through the entire operation. The architect is personally responsible, and should, of course, be held so.

Without an architect the building progresses exactly as a ship at sea with no one at the steering wheel. Few people can even visualize size, let alone form; fewer still know anything at all about detail. Not one in a thousand knows good building from bad; and not one in ten thousand knows or can produce, even when he knowSy the qualities that give a house personality and charm. Any builder can put up a hard block of a house that looks as though made of cast iron or tin. Only an architect of talent (or an owner of genius) can produce the subtleties of line and proportion that alone create a building of beauty.

Thousands of houses of charm — one might almost say the majority of those that have most charm — are furnished without the services of a decorator; but to build a house without an architect is another matter. If you, as an amateur, have ever spent days of intensive thought and effort trying to draw a perfect plan — let alone an exterior to fit the plan — and then had a really good architect in a few moments reshape your plan and obviate each of your difficulties as though by magic, you will understand why you should have your house built by a good architect.

True, all architects are not good ones! Not by any means! And bad ones are a total loss! Moreover, a poor or inexperienced architect gets possibly the same fee as the best one. Bad ones may be very charming neighbors or friends, or relatives. It is difficult to discriminate against one who is a

near neighbor or a dear friend, in favor of a stranger who is nothing to you at all; but, after all, delight in the comfort and beauty of your home surroundings is too vitally important to risk, even to neighborly interest or dear friendship. Surely this is a sufficient reason why you should choose an architect whose work you like, and not let liking for a man whose work you don’t like warp your judgment.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
Quite aside from a question of taste, business relationships are best kept on a business basis. It is much better to keep Jim your friend, apart from his profession, than to make him your architect and be miserable about a dozen things that you cannot bear to tell him because he is your friend. It is very hard to say: "Jim, I think less than nothing of the way your are looking after our job!” But you can say to a total stranger: "Mr. Blank, we are not satisfied with the supervision that has been given our house. "Whoever is to blame for the plastering will have to have it redone.” Or: "The wood that is being used for the Ubrary paneling will all have to come down.” Or — and much worse: "The roof line is very stiff and awkward; it is not a bit like the picture you made of it.”

Nothing like this may occur, it is true; the house from beginning to end may progress without a flaw or hitch. The probabilities in that direction, however, are not strong. In building, it is almost inevitable that there will be a certain number of mistakes, delays, additional charges; these are readily handled on a business basis, but may easily create an uncomfortable strain on an old friendship.

Remember also that architects are more or less specialists. Some have genius for gigantic buildings, some have a beautiful knowledge of a definite style. One man’s taste is for the picturesque, another’s for the severely classic, a third is happiest in a city house plan, a fourth specializes in country places, a fifth builds nothing but Spanish houses.

If you are building a small or medium-sized house it will be necessary to select an architect who lives within a reasonable distance, or who has other work in your neighborhood.

because the cost of overseeing a small building from a great distance is obviously out of all proportion. This consideration is, of course, apart from the still more essential requirement that your architect be one whose special taste expresses your own. If possible, you should consult him before the land is bought, so that he may give his advice on the suitability of the site, both as to beauty and as to the natural adaptability of its conformation and exposure. He would be able to point out, for instance, that while the north slope of a mountain may overlook an entrancing view, the sunless exposure would make an appealing house impossible there — unless you prefer perpetual shade. He might also call your attention to important considerations of cost, such as the fact that foundations on steep hillsides are always expensive. Foundations on rocky mountainsides, I may add, are liable to cost fabulous sums. Foundations on flat sandy land are least expensive — unless in a quicksand district. Friends of my own, who bought a beautiful shore-front site, found a quicksand in the very place where the cellar was to go. It drank up thousands of dollars before bridging methods were found that were secure enough to assure the safety of the house. This, however, was an unusual experience.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
The first thing that the architect will want to know is how big a house you must have, and what are the requirements necessary for your convenience and comfort. It is very necessary for him to know whether you run your household according to fastidious standards or whether you live in the way known as "simple.” It might also be well to ask your definitions of the words "fastidious” and "simple.” Do you want a little room or a big one set apart in perpetually perfect order for the reception of friends or acquaintances? Must there be a study for your husband, a play-room for your children, or are you willing to have whoever-it-may-be come into the living-room where you or various members of

your family may be cluttering up desk or tables with any of the many writing, pasting, sorting or game-playing pursuits? Would you be comfortable in one big informal living-room to sit in, and eat in, and dance in, too? Or must you have a dining-room that will seat twelve, eighteen, twenty-four or more? In this case do you prefer a formal drawing-room of size and a snug little book-room to sit in when alone? Or, on the other hand, would you be content with a small-sized sitting-room and a tiny dining-room to seat no more than six at a pinch?

Are you going to fill your house with so many objects of virtu and so much furniture of tender fragility that the dusting and polishing of each of these treasures will take many hours of one person’s time every day? Or are your rooms going to be fairly empty so that sufficient dusting can be done in scarcely any time at all? In other words, shall you need many servants’ rooms, or few, or one, or none at all?

Do you want people passing by to be impressed by the size of your house — and its cost — or do you prefer to have its street view present as inconspicuous an effect as possible? Do you love beauty of interior for the pleasure it gives you personally? How do you spend your time? Do you read much? Do you play cards much? Do you have much company, and if so, of what sort? Must each member of the family have a room and bathroom of his own? Must you have closet room for endless clothes and personal possessions, or will a dozen hangers be more than enough? How much silver must you find safe or shelf room for? How much linen do you use? How many servants must be provided for? How much space is required for special storage, games or hobbies?

The answers to these questions naturally determine the size of house necessary to your comfort. The next question is that of style.

WHICH STYLE OF HOUSE?

If you are entirely uncertain — perhaps somewhat confused by thinking of "styles” as a series of chronologically selected details, grouped and catalogued according to the when and where of their origins — this question may be much easier to answer if you merely divide all styles of architecture into five general physical types:

1. The Severe Formal.

2. The Minor Formal.

‘ 3. The Balanced Picturesque.

4. The Irresponsible Picturesque.

5. The Blank-Face.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
The outstanding characteristic of the Formal house is undeviating regularity. A line drawn perpendicularly through the center of its front elevation will go directly through the center of the front door and every detail on one side is repeated in exact reverse on the other. In fact, it is a drafting-room custom to draw only one-half of the facade, and, holding a strip of mirror on the center line, let the reflection complete the design. Houses that belong in this category may be either rectangular E-shaped or H-shaped, half H, or three-block English, Italian, French, or American Georgian. The Formal house requires an absolutely flat setting, which may be an artificially built terrace or platform, or may be a natural park or table-land.

T he Minor Formal means merely a simple house of unpretentious size that is evenly balanced in design. Thousands of small houses that have a door in the middle and one or two evenly balanced windows on either side, with regularly spaced windows above, should sit tranquilly also on platforms of land.

The Balanced Ficturesque is suitable to all hillsides. By "balance” is not meant "repetition,” but adjustment of height to weight. A house should give the feeling that its balance is comfortably secure. Its heaviest — central — weight

is placed either on the crown of the hill, with supporting wings packed close against it, or on the middle level with a lower wing on the higher, and a smaller but steeper wing (or possibly a tower) on the lower. The roof of the largest unit is slightly higher than those of the smaller units, but the general outline follows the contour of the hillside against which it is placed. Such houses are sometimes built of stucco or half-timber, but the finest examples are usually of stone that is natural to the location. They include English Tudor, replicas or adaptations suggestive of the Feudal French, German (Rhine castles) , Flill-Town Italian, or our own American rendering of moss-and-lichen-covered graystone. Although especially suited to wooded-hill surroundings, these houses may quite perfectly be placed on level ground and are for that reason fair more adaptable than the inflexibly Formal house, which must never be thrust upon stilts on one side, with chin dug into the earth on the other.

The Irresponsible Picturesque includes every low, unassuming building which, pretending to neither style nor form, can literally perch or huddle or ramble at will almost anywhere; in a meadow or on a hillside, on a sand-dune or in the woods. Its type includes the Spanish hacienda, a collection of small buildings unevenly surrounding a central courtyard. It also includes all dwellings of styleless category, built in irregular units or composed of a multiplicity of wings and galleries; or a collection of log cabins or farm buildings grouped closely together or connected by galleries or colonnades.

The Blank-Face includes every house that turns its back to the street, or that surrounds itself in Spanish, Chinese or other Far-East fashion with blank walls. Many important houses of the old nobility on the left bank of the Seine in Paris do this. On the street, there is nothing to be seen but a high wall with an ordinary or even shabby little workman’s house which is entered through big wooden doors. But when the doors are opened to you, you see a neat porter’s lodge on the inside, and find yourself in a garden facing a beautiful

Peabody, Wilson tfe Brown, Architects

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
section: A DIGNIFIED AND HOMELIKE HOUSE OF THE COLONIAL TYPE
text:
house entirely hidden from the street. This same intention, though somewhat differently expressed, is found in the city or suburban house that has a perfectly plain fagade set flat to the street, with a front door on one side, a kitchen door on the other, and as many windows as need be with straight hanging curtains. Houses of this type are rapidly growing in popularity in America. By means of slight detail and characteristic doors and windows, almost any type of architecture might be indicated in conformity with neighboring houses. The kitchen and all other service rooms would face the street, while the living rooms of the family would face toward a garden at the back.

If the house is plain and the plot is wide, a high wall continues the facade on either side, and a door in this wall should lead by way of a kitchen yard into the kitchen. But if there is no side lot, the kitchen door opens on the same fagade as the front door.

This turning of the house front-side to the back is greatly to be commended, since the fagade overlooking the garden allows an architect infinitely greater possibilities for the development of charm and beauty than a fagade on the street. Moreover, a plain exterior that says nothing about the beauty within is always sympathetic to best taste, whereas an outside ornamented for show and an interior that is neglected or cheap is like nothing so much as a woman in a sable coat and ninety-eight-cent underclothes.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
Let us say you own a piece of property that has a flat plateau, and below it a second table-land. Here is an ideal site for an Italian house; the house on the upper terrace, walled or balustraded, and the garden spread below. But suppose that you are an out-and-out American, that you live in characteristically American style, and that Itahan surroundings — even cypress-spired gardens — would "say nothing” to you. In that case an Italian villa is not for you; it would be idiotic to suppose that a misfit setting, no matter how beautiful it nught in itself be, could ever produce perfection.

Far, far better build a low, rambling American house with these or those characteristics — whichever best suit the type of person you are. Build the house on the upper terrace with a fenced-in flower garden around it, and turn the lower terrace into a tennis court or a swimming pool — or both. Or, if the difference in height is not great, put the house on the lower level and make a garden with a plunge pool, if possible, reached easily by steps going up from the first and down from the second floor.

But, whatever you do — if you really want a house of charm do not be hidebound and imagine you have to build the sort of house the obvious person would put on such a site. Unless you are an obvious person!

Or suppose, on the other hand, you love a French house but hate a French garden. Then don’t have such a garden. Don t think of having it! If the landscape gardener says you

must, get another landscape gardener with more ingenuity and sense. With clever adaptation you can have anything you want — that is, almost anything — except deformity, or a red and yellow Spanish house in the heart of a New England town!

architect’s drawing of the plans

When the site has been bought, the size of the house determined, and its style and material chosen, the architect will submit a plan of each floor and draw or paint a picture — called a rendering — of the house as it is going to be.

It must be confessed that this portrait is apt to be somewhat flattering, much as a fashion-plate drawing is inhumanly slenderized and lengthened; the drawing of a house, on the contrary, is lowered, the lines softened, and floral decoration artfully placed. A photograph (later) of the actual house will be harder, higher and sharper in outline. On the other hand, the straight, hard elevation drawings of the front and back and each side that are always included with the final floor plans (and are used by the contractor to build by) are drawn without perspective or the softening values of light and shade, and look much harder than the actual house ought to. Elevation, cross-sections, and especially drawings of full-sized details are quite unintelligible to the average client, who can only "see a picture,” and to whom all working drawings are unmeaning.

Very important public buildings are always — and private houses are sometimes — modeled in plaster or wax or other materials by people who make these miniature models of houses as a profession. Such models are necessarily very expensive. But if you can draw straight lines with a ruler, or even fairly straight ones — in other words, if you are at all adept in the use of a pencil, paint-brush, glue and scissors, a little paper model drawn to one-eighth of an inch scale is not unreasonably hard to make, and very helpful when you cannot quite see how the house will look.

6S

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
section: A GLANCE AT THE PRACTICAL SIDE OF BUILDING
text:
Let US return to the architect, and take up considerations of cost. When you have determined the size the house must be, and have bought the land, and have decided upon the style of the house you prefer, the chances are — alas! — that your estimate of cost is only one-half, possibly only one-ithird, of what must be allowed for the size and style of house you have in mind.

If you say nothing about cost, and the architect neglects to mention this most necessary detail, the result is apt to be a site for sale, and an architect’s bill for drawings disputed!

But in the usual situation you name the sum you expect to spend and the architect explains that the style or size you describe will cost double your price, whereupon the sum must be increased or cost of building reduced. In the end a compromise is usually arrived at. But if the architect is young or money-conscienceless, he designs a house regardless of the amount you named — and meant — taking it for granted that you will gladly pay for what you want. Maybe you will, maybe you won’t, maybe you can’t.

If an architect knows a man to be enormously rich, he may let his plans run over the amount at first discussed, in order to give him what he feels sure would be more satisfactory. Not because he wants to run up the price and thereby increase his own commission, but because, when he draws the plan, he sees the opportunity to create beauty or comfort or durability that — to one who can afford it — may be well worth the difference in the cost.

When he shows the drawings to the owner, he naturally explains what he has done. If the owner agrees, the details are included in the final drawings; if not, they are reduced in size or quality, or taken out. On the other hand, if the architect knows that the sum the owner specified is all that he can afford to pay, he must check his dreams of perfection, and try only to get the utmost beauty and comfort to be had for the sum available.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
Misleading one’s architect is for this reason a mistake. The make-believe-poor, rich man, gets a substitute house, with which he is afterwards dissatisfied. The make-beUeverich, poor man, is ever afterwards dissatisfied likewise, because of the necessary cutting down of the plans that entranced him and that he was unable to have.

Misunderstandings of cost are not always the fault of the architect (nor of the builder) . If a stranger going into an architect’s office tells him he wants a French Renaissance house and gives him a list of twenty-odd rooms that must be large and high-ceilinged, with ten baths and other details that indicate no evidence of economy, and takes him out in a very expensive car to look at an important site, and says nothing whatever about the cost, a young unthinking architect, taking it for granted that a business man knows what such a project necessarily mounts to, makes a preliminary sketch and floor-plans for a house that will cost in the neighborhood of a hundred thousand dollars probably more. He is quite as bewildered when told by the owner that half of that amount is the utmost sum permissible, as the owner is to hear that what he wants is not to be thought of for twice his intended outlay. A more experienced architect would have avoided such a misunderstanding, perhaps by starting a dialogue such as this:

Architect: "You know, of course, that a house of — let us see, twenty rooms, built of limestone, with enrichment of ornamentation, and with a slate roof, will run well past a hundred thousand for the building — apart from decorations of the interior. Is that all right?”

Client: "Not right at all!”

Architect: "What price had you in mind?”

Client: "Fifty thousand is the utmost that I will spend

on the house, including a garage.”

Architect: "Then you will have to build a very different

type of house.”

Client thereupon builds a stucco or wooden house, with rather simple interior, or else reduces the house in size — or gives up the project of building.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
It is difficult, on the other hand, for an architect to estimate exactly. But he must be either irresponsible or inexperienced not to be able to come within a fair approximation; in fact, you can easily make a rough estimate by determining the cubic footage of the building, and multiplying it by the probable cost of its type of construction. In a location where labor is highest, and for completely fireproof construction, such as apartments and office buildings in New York City, one must allow from seventy to seventy-five cents a cubic foot. In the country, where building materials are local or easily available, the price for a simple frame house can be as low as forty cents — possibly even lower — s. cubic foot. A house twenty-five feet wide by fifty feet long with a sevenfoot cellar, nine-foot first floor, and eight-foot dormered second floor allowing a foot each for cellar, first and second floors — would figure out about as follows: Height, 7 plus 9 plus 8 plus 3, equals 27, which, multiplied by 25 (width), equals 675, and this, multiplied by 50 (length), equals 33,750 cubic feet, which, at thirty-five cents a foot, equals $11,812.50. This would be the least amount possible, and, of course, is exclusive of paint — which is considered decoration and is usually extra. The most expensive construction would come to $23,625, and other specifications would come variously between.

It might be well to attempt some such calculation as this before deciding to build at all. Also, before consulting an architect, you should make a careful list of your personal requirements. Unless you do this you will forget to mention half of the details you "cannot live without,” the architect will omit them from his preliminary plans, and you will be shocked by their additional cost.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
The additional costs because of "extras,” which nearly every house-builder experiences, can be overcome in but one way: study the plans, visualize the details thoroughly before the contracts are let, and then make no changes. It is the endless adding of this item or that, that runs up the bills like boiling-over coffee.

"While we are about it, let us make the house two feet longer, let us have the windows six inches wider. Two feet canH cost much! Six inches are scarcely enough to bother about.” And yet — two feet added to a frame house of average construction, forty feet long and two stories high, will cost about two thousand dollars more, counting only fifty cents a cubic foot, and three to four thousand for a house of more expensive construction. The original windows were probably to be of "stock” size; adding six inches is not merely a question of so many inches of glass and frame, but an alteration in manufacture which exacts that they be hand-made, one by one, instead of machine-made in quantity, and therefore obviously cheaper.

Remember also that everyone from the architect down to the workmen’s helpers is apt to underestimate both time and amount of material, and the resulting cost. This, of course, is true of all of us, and in every situation in life. It always takes longer to do whatever we are doing than we think it is going to, unless it is part of a daily (and therefore timed) routine. This, therefore, is of utmost importance: either hiild your hotise according to a definite contract, and make no changes, or be prepared to pay more than the average person would expect or imagine. Remember that every shelf put up, every hook, rod, fixture, cupboard or coat of paint — every item of decoration, floor polish or linoleum laying, electric fixtures, special hardware, mantles, additional quarter-round of wood, whether added to cornice or to wall — ^is an extra if it was not itemized in the original contract.

It is the architect’s duty to tell the client this or that extra

will cost so much more. Generally he does. But unless each extra is written down, signed for and clipped to the contract — as it should be — ^the client has not the slightest idea that the cost is boiling over until he has paid out the amount of the original estimate, and finds that there is anywhere from ten to fifty per cent, additional cost still due.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
section: HOW TO KEEP WITHIN THE ESTIMATE
text:
If you make no changes the builder cannot charge more than the amount specified in his signed contract. Personally I have known of but two owners who made no changes. The first accepted the architect’s plans for the house, including its interior decoration, much of its furnishings and all of its domestic equipment, signed the bids of the contractor and the landscape architect, and then sailed for Europe and never even wrote a letter about the work. ^JC^hen he returned the entire place was completed, even to the unpacking of items of furniture which had been collected in Europe.

The other client stayed in the neighborhood, but made only one minor change, for which a clause in writing was added to the builder’s contract. In both cases the final bills were necessarily identical with the amounts agreed upon in the contracts.

One of the reasons for extra costs is that many owners cannot visualize the house from a plan, so that when its walls are up (it always looks half its size in rough plaster) he insists upon enlarging this and changing that, without giving a thought to the hours of labor and items of material that are mounting and mounting. Persons to whom mere figures— so many by so many feet— mean nothing, should have the sizes explained to them by measuring rooms that they are at present living in; closets, bathrooms, and all other details should be gone into, especially for a house that is small. The architect, to whom a plan is far more distinct than a finished building, rarely if ever understands that a client, no matter how much he looks at the plans, may quite possibly visualize

almost nothing, and therefore begins to make changes after the walls are up !

However, let us go back to the beginning, and follow the procedure of building in detail. Before making one decision as to location, style, or size, the average property owner must first make his arrangements for financing the enterprise.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
To the inexperienced, the very word "mortgage” brings to mind the favorite plot of melodrama — the "old home” sold over the heads of the aging mother and father by the flint-hearted rich man who holds them in his power by means of the fatal mortgage.

To mortgage your home in order to buy a pleasure car or to take a trip abroad — unless the first is to further the family’s bread-winning assets, such as a car for a physician, or the second is to make the necessary preparation for a career, such as that of an artist or architect — is to court the melodrama’s danger in earnest. But to finance the building of one’s home by means of a mortgage or building loan is to do something that is done by at least ninety-eight persons out of every hundred.

In fact, all business men — even those who can easily, if they choose, pay for the building many times over — prefer to finance the operation rather than tie up that amount of capital in a form that will make it inactive. And for the countless salaried business men and women who earn good incomes, but who have little or no capital, building a house to be paid for in instalments is far more practical than continuing to pay rent, since the renter has no prospect of betterment — ever.

In order to build, it is necessary to have a certain amount of ready cash to start with, the amount depending upon the prospects of the property, and upon whether you have a fixed permanent mortgage or a building loan. In the first case, you can borrow as much as fifty per cent, of the selling price

from any bank. This leaves the other fifty per cent, to be paid in cash at the outset, from your own savings. If you are going to buy an old house to improve, the bank may lend you as much as sixty or seventy per cent, of the cost, if the improvements are extensive and the bank considers that you have greatly enhanced the value of the property.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
A permanent mortgage is one that runs for a long period at an unchanging rate. When it finally comes due, the bank may be willing to renew it — if the value of your property has been kept up — but is sure to demand a reduction of the principal if the mortgage was for as much as half of its original value and the property has run down. This type of mortgage, if too large, is therefore obviously dangerous.

The other type of mortgage, known as an amortizing mortgage, and available through reputable building and loan associations, will let you have a loan amounting to sixty per cent. — sometimes even seventy or eighty per cent. — of the value of a well-built structure in a location of especially good promise. An amortizing mortgage of this kind is paid off gradually at stated intervals — exactly as payment is made for anything else on the instalment plan. You pay, usually, twelve per cent, a year on the amount of the mortgage. Six per cent, of this is interest on the money borrowed, and the other six per cent, is paid-back principal.

In other words, if you borrow ten thousand dollars, you pay twelve hundred dollars the first year; six hundred dollars in interest, which is rent of money, instead of ordinary rent of house, and six hundred is paid back on the mortgage. So that at the beginning of the second year you have a mortgage on your house of nine thousand four hundred dollars instead of ten thousand. The amount of the amortization varies from as little as two per cent., on business buildings, to as high as ten per cent, on dwellings and apartment buildings, but the average amount paid by "home builders” is six per cent.

Although it is usually best to own the house you live in, it might be well — in order to make sure you are wise in buying rather than renting — to do a sum in simple arithmetic, because situations vary and advantage is sometimes on the renting side. If, for instance, you are paying $1000 a year rent on a piece of property worth $20,000, you are paying only five per cent, on the actual capital invested, and the landlord, while receiving only five per cent, gross, is paying at least $600 a year in taxes and repairs. In other words, he is receiving only $400 net — or two per cent. — on his investment. In this case you would be idiotic to change places with him.

But if you are paying $1000 a year on a house worth $10,000 the case is different. While you would have to pay a higher rental to buy it, the rent would decrease slightly each year, and at the end of a set period you would own your house outright. And if you are paying $1000 a year rent on property worth $5000, the sooner you become its owner the better. In other words, the desirability of owning increases as the value of the investment decreases in proportion to the rental.

Suppose that you are paying $1200 rent on a $12,000 valuation, and that you have only $2000 saved as a building fund. A loan association, however, is willing to let you borrow $10,000 on the property. If you take that loan and buy the house, your rent is increased to $1500 the first year, and each year thereafter decreases slightly. Taking the sum of $10,000 that you borrow as an approximate figure (because it is the easiest sum to figure on), and supposing that the house and land will cost $12,000 complete, the table of the operation will be as follows:

After the seventeenth year the expense of buying is ended, and the house is owned in full.

The amounts allowed for repairs in this case are rather low; but on the other hand, those of a small house, whose owner is capable of making minor ones himself, may not be even as high as noted. Repairs and interest are a little like a seesaw; as one goes up, the other comes down. A new house, if at all well built, should have no repairs of any account. As the interest decreases, the repairs grow larger, so that the one is somewhat offset by the other.

The foregoing table merely indicates what it would cost — plus barest fixed charges — to buy a $12,000 house on which you borrow $10,000. If you borrow less, your payments are less; or if you keep a permanent mortgage, as noted in the first instance, you pay six per cent, on the money borrowed without adding the six per cent, for paying off any part of it. Your interest on $10,000 is fixed at $600 a year. Or on a $10,000 house for which you pay $5000 in ready cash and $5000 in borrowed money, the interest on the loan is $300 a year. Your rent is represented at $600, however, because you should allow for the interest lost on the $5000 cash you put in.

A house costing $120,000 would multiply every figure by ten, while a little bungalow costing $1200 would divide by ten instead. If the amortization on $10,000 is ten per cent, instead of six, you pay $1000 "on instalment” and $600 for

interest, the first year. The second year you pay on $9000, and so on.

At all events the loan — whether large or small — is arranged by your real estate agent; or if you own the land, the bank will make the loan for you.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
There is another way to pay for your house gradually, without doing any "financing” at all — but only if the size of your family permits, and if the house you are building is larger than your minimum need. Of course, if your family consists of many members who cannot be packed into less space than you have allowed for in the finished building, borrowing on an amortizing mortgage is the best answer to your problem. Or if, for reasons of your own, you choose to keep a fixed mortgage of from thirty to forty per cent, of the value of the house on your building, that, as already noted, is a sound procedure. But if, on the other hand, you are a family of two — newly married, perhaps — no way of acquiring a home is as sound and as economical as that of building by instalments.

This means building the least amount of your house that you can manage to be half-way comfortable in, and completing it part by part as you save. In the bank-loan method, you get what you want to start with, and pay afterwards, little by little, plus interest — which at six per cent, on $10,000 totals $5304 — or more than half again as much as the amount borrowed. In building part by part, these interest charges are saved, the house is cleared of debt sooner, but you have to wait for its completion instead of getting it at once.

Or suppose you do not wish to borrow any money. You have six thousand dollars and are going to build a six thousand dollar house instead of the ten thousand dollar one you want (or any other amount — the sum does not matter) . It would be far better to build a first unit of your ultimate ideal

than to build at once a completed but inadequate house that is not at all what you really like, and that can never be made into anything different.

If you are going to adopt this course, you naturally explain your intention to your architect, so that he can make his design with this end in view. Unlimited varieties of plans and exterior beautifully adapt themselves to this sort of instalment building, but there are certain unelastic others that do not take kindly to piecemeal building, either without or within.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
section: SOME HINTS ON THE PIECEMEAL PLAN
text:
And yet the best way to approach this method of building is first to complete the plans of the eventual house, exactly as you hope some day to have it, and then to begin with the barest essentials. If you are going to have a coal range, it is doubly necessary to build the kitchen. On the other hand, if you are going to use oil or gas or electricity to cook with, the future pantry might serve as temporary kitchen. Or if you build the permanent kitchen with chimney for the range, the pantry of the future is perhaps used as a dining alcove, to be closed off later from the dining-room — which is now serving as the living-room. In this selection, be sure to lay the piping for the future pantry’s sink.

Or possibly you build the front hall and stairs before completing the back; or perhaps your original entrance is a side or rear one, and back stairs serve to take you up to your present sleeping quarters, which will some day be the servant’s wing.

Or perhaps you choose — and are able — to build the front hall and permanent stairway and your own bedroom with bath (or baths) , closets, and sleeping porch complete. Perhaps you build the big living-room at once, in which you eat as well as live, and have a small temporary kitchenette that later is to become a lavatory and coat-room.

But however much you build, it must be divided ver-

tically — never horizontally — into sections. Each unit must be built from cellar to roof. In other words, never build a bungalow, intending later to add a second story which will necessitate tearing off the roof and building a new one. You can leave second-story space, if desired, in the shape of an unfinished attic ; but ceiling height, windows and dormers should be put in at the beginning.

Wherever a room or other addition is to go, the connecting door frame must be set and temporarily plastered in, so that no future tearing out of walls need be resorted to; and of course all piping and wiring must be laid, and preparation for future connections boxed in on the outside, so that when new building is in progress, wires and pipes are all at hand without coming into the rooms you are living in.

There is one quite inevitable trick of the imagination that offsets impatience, and even to a great degree mitigates the makeshift of those who must look forward rather long to the completion of their some-day house — which is that the vision of the house is inevitably supplied by the blank doors, the beam-supported wall-space roughly plastered over, but ready to be broken through the moment the room or hall or loggia on the other side is ready and waiting.

Irregular styles of architecture lend their help somewhat better to unit-by-unit building than do those which are very regular.

The English house of the general Tudor type, or the simple farm-house type of building, is pliant, tractable and amiably yielding to the retrenchment or enlargement of its owner’s needs. It is especially suitable for the plan that is to be completed in sections, since one complete building can be added to, by indefinite numbers of sister buildings. The blockshaped Georgian, or any type of Formal house, on the other hand, looks maimed if built only in part, and lends itself no better to afterthought additions.

About the only way to plan for a Formal house to be built piecemeal is to begin with a central block and add a wing first on one side and then later on the other. Or even

begin with a wing and a slice of the back, putting on the front next and the balancing wing last.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
section: AGAIN WE RETURN TO THE ARCHITECT
text:
\

Apart from making a suitable plan for unit building, financial arrangements are entirely outside of the province of the architect, although it is ethically his duty to see that you are given best value for what you spend on building and on whichever part of the decoration he designs. You must be sure, therefore, to fit into the total sums you have arranged for, a margin for extras, for furnishing, and for putting the grounds in order, and for the architect’s- fee, which is usually from six to ten per cent, of the total cost of the building that he has designed. This includes excavations, grading — only in so far as it is preparation as a foundation for the house — all building by carpenters, masons, brick-layers, plumbers, electricians, and the work of painters on the exterior and on the architectural decorations of the interior.

If the architect completes the structural decoration of the rooms — which he should — or designs the garden, which he does rarely, except for very important Italian gardens or Spanish patios which are fundamentally architectural, these items are also included in the total on which he gets ten per cent.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
The least expensive material that can be used is wood (barring adobe in desert sections). The cheapest construction is that which is most like a box. Bay windows, dormers — all things that cut into or stand out from wall or roof surfaces — add to the cost of construction.

The house of greatest beauty at least expense is the "frame house” with either shingle or clapboard walls and shingle roof. The frame house includes every variety of Colonial that is not of brick, as well as endless varieties of "just houses”

and bungalows. Log cabins are cheap only when built in a forest of pine or spruce or other tall, straight-growing trees.

The frame house of highest type is built of brick or hollow tile covered with wood, and has a well-bred quality of being better than it pretends. The reverse of this construction is the house of brick veneer over an under-frame of wood. There is no actual objection to this, however, even though it lacks the ethical quality of the reverse just noted.

Woods vary in value from spruce and fir to cedar and oak for use on the exterior, and from fir and pine to oak and mahogany, walnut, cypress, maple, and pine for the interior. They vary, moreover, in quality from planks of rough and porous surface that splinter into hang-nails and drink paint or stain like a sponge — and so unevenly that the finished result looks woolly — to fine woods of firm and even surface that in time becomes as smoothly glazed as Chinese porcelain.

There should be no fear as to the durability of wood. It will last, at all events, for a dozen generations, which is longer than the house-builder or his children or grandchildren need worry about. It is true, wooden roof-shingles have to be replaced every twenty years, and wooden steps about every other spring; but they are exceptions. I would recommend that front steps be of brick or stone as a measure of economy, since wooden steps get down at heel with amazing facility. But wooden repairs are inexpensive when continuously attended to. A frame house will tumble to pieces if not looked after, but so will a neglected brick house, or even a stone one.

Stucco over hollow tile is of about the same cost as either combination of wood and brick. Stucco over wire lath fastened to wood-frame costs considerably less, and, properly done, is usually quite satisfactory. But if one can afford to pay the difference, hollow tile is much to be preferred, not only because it is fireproof but because it is practically an insurance against cracking, which is the flaw of stucco when applied to an unstable foundation.

The walls of nearly all Italian and Spanish houses, and of nearly all "apparently” open-timbered Normandy cottages

and English houses, as well as those of endless other varieties, are of stucco with roofs of tile (real or composition) . Several modern renderings in stucco of Colonial, including Georgian, have been very successful — especially when the stucco surface is almost plaster-fine.

Brick is higher in cost than tile and stucco. The cost of brick increases according to quality, and according to whether the brick-yard is at a distance or near by.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
The price of all building material is greatly increased if brought by freight; a fact easily understandable if one considers the weight, for instance, of even the very smallest brick house! Fortunately, the ordinary pinkish "common” brick is often far more beautiful in its porous surface, varying color, and faculty for acquiring the "softened look of age” because of its tendency when close to the ground to acquire a tinge of — let us call it patina. More expensive bricks are sometimes beautiful but quite as often they are merely hard and tight-grained and sharp-edged and as beautifying as blocks of iron.

As for the threatening Persian Invasion of black bricks, brown bricks, maroon bricks, and leanings toward patterns and shadings and blendings of peacock and yellow and rose and green — such ingredients do not make beautiful houses, but hideosities. Therefore, let us copy gardens and murals from the Persians, but leave their bricks alone!

Stone — The cost of stone is much higher than of brick — unless poor stone- work is taken in comparison with best brick- work. Smooth-finished stone is the most expensive material (next to marble) that there is. The rougher the stone, and the more local its nature, the less the cost. In localities where field-stone abounds, especially when it is found on the same property, a house of stone can be built at a very reasonable cost in the way known as rubble. (Do not confuse rubble with "cobble.” Rubblework has great charm, whereas round, rain-washed stones jutting out from the walls like pans full of biscuits are an offense to good taste.)

The cost of stone naturally increases enormously in pro-

portion to its distance from the quarry and to the method of setting. Walls of evenly squared stones beautifully mortised mount up to many times the cost of those which are built of irregularly dressed field-stone, set into a wall of mortar like plums in a pudding.

Mountain graystone or granite that must be quarried is always expensive — but magnificently durable. The cost of steel-frame, hollow-tile and concrete construction, with stone facing and with stone or slate or tile roof, runs from about eighty cents a square foot — with wood-trim — to a dollar, even a dollar and a half or more, for a house of great elaboration of detail, such as certain Tudor country estates of marked magnificence.

WHAT PRICE TUDOR?

The Enghsh Tudor house of perfectly imitated old weathered stone, with rain-and-wind-polished carving, and patined metal, has been achieved in many examples by one of to-day’s greatest architects — but at a PRICE! Very straightforward rough-dressed stone houses with wood-trim and first-class fireproof roof can be built as low as seventy cents a cubic foot. Brick for about sixty cents. These figures are merely approximate, because details of finish and of location greatly affect the cost.

Half-Timber — Real half-timber with brick nogging is very expensive — even as expensive as stone. "Real” open timber means that the studs and beams and supports are set up of solid wood (weathered oak usually) with their front faces left exposed and the spaces between filled in with brick, laid in various patterns.

Imitation half- timber houses are built of stucco, and then boards stained dark are put on top of the stucco in imitation of actual timber construction.

The most expensive building material is marble — very rarely chosen for a complete house, but often used for part, or all, of the trim of Georgian houses of brick. Trim includes

quoins — blocks of marble set into the brick corners, originally devised to interlock right-angled walls (as in any small wooden box) , but now merely ornamental.

The less expensive brick house has doors and trim and quoins of wood, painted white.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
The materials of the exterior necessarily influence the cost of the interior. A brick-and-marble Georgian house would naturally promise a lovely oval or double, or that most beautiful feature of a Colonial interior, the free-standing stair; spacious, high-ceilinged rooms with elaborate cornices and trim; paneled walls and marble — or hand-wrought wood — mantles. Stone and half- timber houses of Tudor or Elizabethan importance presuppose an important and richly carved staircase of pollard oak, and high wainscoted rooms and open-timbered ceiling. Real open-timbered ceilings show the actual floor beams overhead, requiring that they be smooth-finished beams instead of the rough-finished boards set edgewise of usual construction. Ceilings are often made of plaster in marvelous imitation of wood.

Italian and Spanish houses are expensive chiefly because of tile roofs, floors, and stair treads, and beautiful wroughtiron work. Roof tiles are pressed one by one over the knees of the workmen who make them. The trim, however, is lacking, doors are often absent, walls are left in the rough.

The least exacting style of house — barring the bungalow— is the simple one of shingles or clapboard with shingle roof and plain board trim inside, and with equally plain furnishing. The utterly primitive house of Tudor example with unpamted open beams, unpainted wood without and within, may easily be quite expensive, since timbers hand-hewn and planed are in this day quite the opposite of reasonable in price. The element of price, indeed, segregates the Tudor, Jacobean, Georgian and French chateau as suitable only for those whose purse is very deep; the tile-roofed Italian, Spanish, and all stone and brick houses as being of considerable outlay ; and houses of wood, of whitewashed field stone, or of stucco with Spanish or Italian accents as being moder-

ate in cost. Houses of wood are cheapest. Every deviation from straight flat walls and straight back and front gable roof adds to cost.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
If you have no architect, you and the contractor build the house, and you assume the responsibility that belongs normally to the architect. But if you employ an architect you have no personal business relations with the contractor except through the architect.

When the architect’s plans have been approved — at his own estimate — and detail drawings have been completed, you and your architect together decide upon the contractor. Sometimes a contractor is selected from the beginning and no "bids” are given out. But more often — especially for a house of any importance — duplicate blue-prints of plans and carbons of specifications are sent out by the architect to several contractors who bid on them, meaning that each names the price at which he is willing to sign a contract to build the house according to the plans and specifications that were sent to him.

The bids, which are received together at a certain hour on a certain day, are always contained in sealed envelopes, and these are opened by the architect in the presence of the owner. The advantages of each are then discussed and one of them is selected.

It is usually supposed that the lowest bidder secures the job, but this is not necessarily true. For instance, if a contractor sends in a bid that is much lower than any other — lower than the architect’s own quite expert calculations make possible — this bidder’s willingness to build at an obvious loss would warrant a close investigation of the matter. One reason might be, in the case of an unusually important job, a legitimate willingness on the part of the builder to stand a loss as a pure matter of advertising, or of keeping his organization going in slender times. He may believe that

his loss on this building will be repaid to him in reputation and future jobs. This reason cannot well be offered, however, in the case of an unimportant house. Another reason is that a builder may be so inexperienced or so incompetent as to make a serious miscalculation.

A third reason is one of which the architect of experience is always chary. A too-low bid from a builder of experience is sometimes an evidence of the unscrupulous contractor who underbids, with intent to freeze out his more conscientious competitors. This type of "squeezer” is usually one who gambles on being able to substitute inferior material and workmanship or to make the extras so numerous and so confusing in their unending repetition of "hours’ labor,” lumber, "hours’ labor,” nails, cement, "hours’ labor,” paint, "hours’ labor,” bricks, "hours’ labor” — page after page — until no one, not even the architect, can make head or tail of it. It is impossible to keep tab on such a builder, unless the house is big enough to pay for a superintendent who never leaves the job and who makes itemized lists of materials and daily time-sheets of "hours’ labor.”

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
Before leaving the subject of costs it might be well to explain a few details of cost to the architect which unaccustomed house-builders rarely take into consideration.

A bill that countless clients consider unfair is the bill for drawings which have to be discarded because the client changes his mind. When an architect makes plans and sketches and they are accepted — even after considerable alteration — the cost is included in the architect’s regulation percentage on the finished building. But when the house is discarded for an entirely new design, or the project possibly is given up altogether, the architect necessarily sends in a bill for office cost in preparing these drawings.

To the inexperienced, this bill often seems enormous and unjust, because not one person in fifty has the least idea — or

stops to think — how much architectural drawings cost. In a business office, the average salary is moderate; many clerks occupy small space, and, as often as not, work by artificial light. An architect’s draftsmen and tenderers are all experts who get high salaries; each must have space for a big drafting table, and brilliant daylight is essential. At present-day rentals, the overhead of a drafting room is appalling. Paper and blue-printing alone are items that run into thousands of dollars a year in an office of average size.

There is another phase of cost- — social wastage, we might call it — to which architects, more than men of other professions, not even excepting lawyers, are subjected. A client calls on a business man or lawyer and discusses business. When the discussion is over, the client leaves. But an architect is, for reasons that have never been explained, looked upon as an addition to the social life of the family. If an architect is agreeable, cultivated, intelligent, as architects are rather notably apt to be; and if he is young, the house-builder assumes that he is his (or more especially her) property.

Let us say, for example, that John Robinson, a young architect of talent, is given the Jones house to build. He is much pleased. Mrs. Jones is a charming woman. Mr. Jones is a likeable man. The house promises to be a good one; moreover, it will help carry office expenses, so that he can work on an important competition, which, should he win it, would "make” him. He will have plenty of time to complete his design for the competition by devoting five or six hours a day to it, until the contest closes. By working ten or at most twelve hours, he can easily (he thinks) take care of the Jones project and continue to superintend the jobs he has in hand — jobs that are small and time-taking. The Jones house is seemingly a gift from Heaven.

And then! Mrs. Jones comes to his office and talks and talks. He finds that she is rather vague, but inclined to like the idea of a frame Colonial house set in a field. So he makes tentative plans of very simple construction. Mrs. Jones is enthusiastic. Mr. Jones thinks they look all right, and asks

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
text:
Robinson how much the house will cost. Robinson says it should cost approximately so much. Mr. Jones is pleased and everything is sunshine. Then, little by little, Mrs. Jones decides she wants a lot of changes, and is entirely indefinite as to what they shall be. She changes her mind about Colonial and thinks she prefers a French house. She has some French chairs and a set of Louis XIV bedroom furniture. The Colonial house is discarded and Robinson designs a double-winged Provengal house. She does not recognize it as "French,” so he sketches a chateau type with high slate roof. She is delighted with the sketch, but seems to understand little or nothing of the plans. He draws sketches of interiors so that she can better understand.

She likes to watch him draw, praises his pencil facility, but seems as vague as ever in her acceptance or rejection of his plans. Gradually she assumes that young Robinson is a species of paid companion. She calls him up at all hours to come at once and decide about the house. When he arrives she talks ten minutes about it and hours about herself, her artistic tastes, her appreciation of the beautiful. What she won’t talk about is how big each room must be, how many rooms she must have, or whether the first, second or third floor plan is satisfactory. Finally, she definitely decides on a stone Cotswold type of house, and, acting on a rather hazy outline of her requirements, the architect designs a house that he thinks would be suitable to the tastes and needs of the Jones family. He completes a set of plans and elevations, spending about six hours in sleep and the other eighteen trying to get the Jones house definitely decided upon, and struggling to finish his drawings for the competition. By this time Mrs. Jones has added innumerable rooms and increased sizes, besides changing from rather primitive wood construction to excessively expensive stone — which is not quarried within hundreds of miles of the Jones location — and Mr. Jones is absolutely aghast at the price. Remembering nothing but the roughly estimated total of the farm-house plan Mr. Jones is convinced that young Robinson is incompetent, if

not wilfully trying to force them to build an unnecessarily expensive house. At all events, negotiations are terminated, and Robinson sends in his bill for costs of rejected drawings, which is protested. Robinson sues; Mr. Jones pays, but Robinson has npt only lost the Jones good-will, but he has also lost his chance in the competition because the Jones house took too much of his time.

This is an extreme example, but cases approaching it can be counted by the hundreds.

One last word from the point of view of the architect: Since the operation of building is essentially a partnership between yourself and him, it is not unreasonable to ask that you give at least a little thought to his side of the case.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter V — If You Are Going to Build
section: WHAT YOU CAN DO FOR OR AGAINST YOUR ARCHITECT
text:
How many times has a house-owner said to you: "The design of the house was entirely my own. I merely had an architect to work out the mechanical details.” Which is very like saying: "I diagnosed appendicitis myself — the surgeon merely operated.”

The worst thing you can do against your architect — something much worse than claiming credit for his design — is to discuss the plans for your house with every friend, neighbor and acquaintance, and change your mind about this detail or that with each opinion.

And what you can do for your architect is to discuss privately all points about which you and your family can’t agree, thresh them out by yourselves, settle them, and then tell him. A still more important thing to do for him is to trust him, and to realize that unless you do, he can’t look after your interests in the way you expect him to, and in the way he has every intention of doing. Moreover, do not put him in a false position by giving direct orders either to the contractors or to their workmen. The architect, who is alone responsible for the success of the building, must be in sole control of the job.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
text:
T^O one who genuinely loves houses — both inside and out — there is no occupation so fascinating as restoring a once beautiful house that has been maimed, or discovering the possibilities in one of seemingly hopeless ugliness, or solving the problem of a honeycomb plan. Of course, the chief attraction of remodeling is not merely that the operation can, in many instances, be attempted by the owner, but that few new houses can compete with the appealing personality of an old one. Not only are its trees and bushes — if it have any! — inimitably becoming, but there are always telltale evidences of its long past — apparent in slightly softened edges of window-frames, chimneys, door-sills and the color of its stone or brick — that are missing in the blank regularities of the house that is still an unprinted page.

The problems of remodeling naturally vary from the simplest ones of making a few interior changes or an addition at the back, to complete remodeling — either in harmony with the original design or in accord with a new design that changes it into a different type of house. Between these two extremes the first of which can be done quite easily by almost any one, and the second of which, if the house is at all important, should be attempted only by an expert — are hundreds of midway remodelings that can be done by almost any owner of cultivated taste assisted by a good builder.

If it is hard for you to see possibilities in imagination, then by all means take an architect with you when you go house-hunting; but if, on the other hand, you are of those who mentally reconstruct every not-pleasing house that you

look at, your difficulty is not likely to be in finding one worth redoing, but in deciding which to choose of the many ’that offer enticing possibilities. If you are looking at this place and at that, however, and have no idea which of several will take most kindly to becoming your home, it may perhaps be easier to make your choice if you realize that houses of definite style, especially formal ones, necessarily exact adherence to the conventions of their types. You can’t tag runways and lean-tos and odd outbuildings to "mansions” of brick and stone or marble. But you can take a barn and a chicken-house and almost any odd farm-building, move them about and put them together in whichever grouping a perceiving eye directs, and achieve a pleasing irregularity that lends itself to delightful planting of other unconventionalities of a similar nature. Moreover, hundreds of insignificant, unpleasing or downright ugly houses can be turned into dwellings of charm — if their proportions are within reason — sometimes even if they are not.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
text:
But let us leave all considerations of outside beauty or ugliness for a later part of this chapter, and begin by assuming that if you are so much interested in a house that you are thinking of buying it, the probabilities are that the outside is attractive as it is. Therefore, let us choose a lovely old Colonial house; and in order to make our first example easy, let us say that its plan is of the hall-through-the-middle and rooms-on-either-side variety; that it looks unattractive because its wall-papers are in varieties of shabby brown, and that it seems uncomfortable because it has neither electric light nor plumbing — but let us add quickly that both are available, (^^e will take up their lack, later.) Even when considering the simplest plan, it is best to lay it out on paper. This is the first thing every architect does; one of the easiest things in the world to do — but one which very few prospective house-buyers ever think of or seem to know

about.

You will need a few sheets of cross-barred paper and a rule or tape measure of some sort; if you buy one, get a

fifty-foot surveyor’s tape that winds up on a covered spool, because it eliminates laying a lot of short rule-lengths end to end across the floor and adding them up in your mind — • with occasional mistakes. ^J^ith a long tape you merely get some one to hold the end at each point that you want to start from, and then the distance to which you pull it out, whatever it may be, is marked in feet and inches. With a two-foot rule you have to add six twos and seventeen; on a surveyor’s tape you read *'13 feet 5 inches.” At all events you measure every wall length and mark it on the crossbarred paper. Regular engineers’ or architects’ paper, subdivided into eighths of an inch, gives you a standard scale; but any sort of cross-barred pad-paper will do, no matter what the size. In any case, you count one square as a foot, and mark the total feet of wall length as so many squares. Put down the exact length of each wall in each room, and the positions of windows and doors. In making this rough "layout” it is not necessary to bother about the thickness of walls except where blocked by a chimney or other obstruction.

It is necessary to measure all irregularities in shape and to put the rooms next to each other as they belong, so that with the plan of each floor (which is automatically accurate) in front of you, you can see the pattern of it as a whole,

and know exactly how much space there is, and how hard _

or how easy— it will be to open doors through, or to add or move partitions, as the need may be.

If it lays itself out” nicely, it may be unnecessary to consult an architect. For instance, let us say that the plan we are considering is about like Figure 38. Then, on the first floor, let us say that we decide merely to knock out the wall between the front and back parlors and to add a sun-porch at the left side, making the most typical modern small-house first-floor plan known. A garage on one side possibly balances the sun-porch on the other— if not spoiling to the kitchen.

Or if there be a garden at the back, it might appeal

to you to change the kitchen and dining-room about; to omit the kitchen-screened porch at the right side, but to put a sun-porch or terrace or both across the back.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
section: TYPICAL PLAN OF HOUSE TO BE REMODELED
text:
For such a simple change of interior as either Figure 39 or Figure 40, an architect would not be necessary; but per-

KllCHCK

Second Floor

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
section: A SIMPLE PLAN FOR REMODELING THE SAME HOUSE
text:
haps if you make as much exterior change as that shown in Figure 41, with the addition of bay windows and two balancing outbuildings, it might be well to consult one — especially if you have to add dormers to the third floor for servants’ rooms, or if you build two-story wings. At all events, with a straightforward plan of the sort that calls for a hall through the middle and rooms on either side, changes are seldom difficult to make.

But a honeycomb plan is quite another story. For instance, a plan that is typical of Colonial New England is shown in Figure 42. This is a big house with twelve bedrooms but with uncomfortably adjusted space from the point of view of modern living. When these houses were built, mother and father occupied the central bedroom, and the children were put in cubicles all around and were unable to get out or come in without going through their parents’ room. Unless you, who buy such a house, use the principal bedroom on the second floor as hall space, there is no way for the occupants of six rooms to get out except through room No. 1 ; and the occupant of No. 8 must pass through No. 7 as well as No. 1. Many houses of this plan have an attic in place of bedrooms 7 and 8. Others have only one floor, but nearly all have the small rooms around the diningroom. In a few examples, the only second-floor room reached by the stairs is No. 2, in which case No. 1 has no direct entrance. Of course, endless solutions are possible according to the needs of the owner. For example, let us say that you need three masters’ rooms, all large, and three servants’ rooms and a guest room. One change would be as in Figure 43.

This or any other plan is capable of being altered into dozens of patterns, though the working out of the inside

Space in the center of the house is apt to be a cause of stumbling.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
section: ONE WAY TO MODERNIZE THE SAME COLONIAL HOUSE
text: These two plans are outlined merely because more typical of the average Colonial or Victorian house than the two which I am choosing to describe in detail, because I designed much of one and all of the other myself.

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
text: A snap-shot of the first is shown in Plate 8. As its picture shows, it was a small, rambling, one-storied, whitepainted, green-shuttered house that sat in a field on top of a slight hill. It had a sign on it "FOR SALE,” and every time

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
text:
we passed it we used to look at it and talk about it and say how enchanting it would be with a lot of flowers around it. But the inside seemed hopeless; a honeycomb plan, ceiling seven feet three inches. Every possibility of opening a wall through was blocked by unused chimneys, and it was too small for us — by five rooms. It had not a single pipe of plumbing, no open fireplaces, no garden, and its chief beauty was its charming lowness, which, should I buy it, I was prepared to destroy by raising the roo*f. To this proposition my son would not listen. He said if I made it higher I would ruin it. Moreover, the main part of the house was over a hundred years old, and the beams were fitted and pegged

HOUSE NUMBER ONE AS IT WAS (See Plate 9 for House as It Now Is)

KITCHEN AS IT WAS (See Plate 42 for Kitchen as It Is) [PLATE 8]

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
section: HOUSE NUMBER ONE AS IT NOW IS
text:
and fourteen inches square; it would be vandalism to cut through construction like that. I might do what I liked, but he would not touch its roof.

Meanwhile I looked at other houses, but always came

back to this one. Finally I took a sheet of cross-barred paper and laid out its plan, which is shown in Figure 44.

A kodak of the second floor will be found in Plate 10. This side of the house is not the one that had the heavy beams, but the photograph shows the side walls, which were over two feet high, so that adding four feet gave us plenty of head-room. I took some snap-shots, scribbled outlines of

heightened roofs, and showed my son the results of my measurings.

So then he solved the lower-floor plan by taking away the front door and putting the entrance at the side. He also designed the door and fitted in the circular stairway, attended

title: The Personality of a House
author: Emily Post
chapter: Chapter VI — The House That You Remodel
text:
to the roof raising, knocked out the two old chimneys and built one new, and then left me to do the rest — which was to fit three bedrooms and two baths into the new upstairs space, make a few changes in the kitchen, riddle the walls with windows, furnish the interior, and plant the garden.
